items.prompt: What is the main body of a moss plant, the part that is green and lives on the ground?

options.label: The capsule
options.feedback: The capsule is the spore-producing tip on a stalk, not the main green body. The main green body is what you see when you look at a moss mat.

options.label: The gametophyte
options.feedback: Correct. The green, leafy part of a moss is called the gametophyte because it carries the sex organs, and it is the everyday plant you see.

options.label: The sporophyte
options.feedback: The sporophyte is the stalk and capsule that grows out of the gametophyte to make spores; it does not live alone as the green body.

options.label: The rhizoid
options.feedback: Rhizoids are the thin, root-like threads that anchor the moss to the ground, not the main green body itself.

items.ok_line: The green mass you see is the gametophyte, the main plant.
items.ko_line: The capsule is only a small spore tip, not the whole plant.
items.exp_text: The gametophyte is the dominant, green, leafy part of a moss. It lives independently, performs photosynthesis, and is the form that most people call a moss. The sporophyte grows from it only to make and release spores.

items.prompt: What part of a moss plant is responsible for anchoring it to the soil or rock it grows on?

options.label: The leaves
options.feedback: Leaves in mosses are small, green flaps that catch light; they do not anchor the plant.

options.label: The stem
options.feedback: The stem holds the leaves up but does not attach the plant to the ground; that job belongs to the root-like threads.

options.label: The capsule
options.feedback: The capsule is the spore-producing tip at the top of the stalk, not an anchor.

options.label: The rhizoids
options.feedback: Correct. Rhizoids are thin, hair-like threads that grow from the base of the moss and cling to the surface, anchoring the plant firmly.

items.ok_line: Rhizoids hold the moss down, like roots do for bigger plants.
items.ko_line: Leaves and stem are for light and support, not attachment.
items.exp_text: Rhizoids are simple, multicellular threads that emerge from the lower part of the gametophyte. They do not absorb much water—they mainly serve to anchor the moss to its substrate, whether that is soil, rock, or tree bark.

items.prompt: What do mosses use to reproduce without flowers or seeds?

options.label: Pollen
options.feedback: Pollen is used by flowering plants to carry sperm between flowers; mosses never produce pollen.

options.label: Seeds
options.feedback: Seeds are a structure of seed plants; mosses do not make them at any stage of their life.

options.label: Spores
options.feedback: Correct. Mosses release countless spores from their capsules, and each spore can grow into a new moss plant under damp conditions.

options.label: Fruits
options.feedback: Fruits are seed-bearing structures of flowering plants; mosses have no fruits whatsoever.

items.ok_line: Mosses spread by releasing spores, not seeds or pollen.
items.ko_line: Mosses are spore plants, so pollen and seeds do not apply.
items.exp_text: Mosses belong to a group of plants that reproduce by spores. A capsule at the top of a stalk releases thousands of tiny spores into the air, and each spore can germinate into a new moss if it lands in a moist, suitable spot.

items.prompt: What is the thin, stalk-like structure that lifts a moss capsule above the green plant?

options.label: The seta
options.feedback: Correct. The seta is the stalk that grows up from the gametophyte and holds the capsule high, helping spores spread in the wind.

options.label: The rhizoid
options.feedback: Rhizoids are thin threads that anchor the moss down; they never lift anything up.

options.label: The leaf
options.feedback: Leaves are flat and green, attached to the stem; they do not hold up a capsule.

options.label: The protonema
options.feedback: A protonema is the early, thread-like stage that grows from a spore before the leafy plant appears, not a stalk.

items.ok_line: The seta is the stalk that raises the capsule into the air.
items.ko_line: Rhizoids anchor; the seta lifts the capsule upward.
items.exp_text: The seta is a slender, erect stalk that connects the gametophyte to the capsule. By lifting the capsule above the moss mat, it allows wind to catch the spores and carry them away more effectively.

items.prompt: What is the early, thread-like growth that appears when a moss spore first germinates?

options.label: A capsule
options.feedback: A capsule forms only later, after the gametophyte has grown; it is not the first stage from a spore.

options.label: A seta
options.feedback: A seta appears only when the sporophyte grows, which is much later; it is not the first growth.

options.label: A rhizoid
options.feedback: Rhizoids are anchors that form on the gametophyte, not the initial growth from a spore.

options.label: A protonema
options.feedback: Correct. A protonema is a branching, thread-like filament that develops first, and then buds to form leafy gametophytes.

items.ok_line: A spore first grows into a thread-like protonema.
items.ko_line: The capsule is a late sporophyte part, not the first growth.
items.exp_text: When a moss spore lands on moist ground, it germinates into a branched, filamentous protonema. This stage looks like green threads and eventually produces buds that develop into the familiar leafy gametophytes.

items.prompt: What is the structure inside a moss capsule that actually contains the spores?

options.label: The seta
options.feedback: The seta is the stalk below the capsule; it does not hold spores.

options.label: The sporangium
options.feedback: Correct. The sporangium is the sac-like structure within the capsule where spores are produced and stored until release.

options.label: The rhizoid
options.feedback: Rhizoids are anchoring threads at the base, not spore holders.

options.label: The leaf
options.feedback: Leaves are photosynthetic organs; they have nothing to do with spore storage.

items.ok_line: The sporangium is the spore-bearing sac inside the capsule.
items.ko_line: The seta is the stalk, not the spore container.
items.exp_text: Inside the moss capsule lies the sporangium—a spherical or cylindrical cavity filled with spores. When the capsule opens, these spores are released to the outside world, ready to start new moss plants.

items.prompt: What do mosses rely on, instead of true roots, to absorb water and minerals?

options.label: Their leaves
options.feedback: Leaves do not absorb water directly; they are thin but the main uptake happens over the whole plant surface.

options.label: Their stems
options.feedback: Stems provide support but are not the main absorptive organs in mosses.

options.label: Their entire surface
options.feedback: Correct. Mosses have no roots; they take in water and dissolved minerals directly through their leaves and stem, aided by capillary action between tightly packed shoots.

options.label: Their capsules
options.feedback: Capsules are for spores, not for water absorption.

items.ok_line: Mosses absorb water and minerals over their whole body.
items.ko_line: Mosses lack roots, so they soak up moisture everywhere.
items.exp_text: Mosses are non-vascular plants, meaning they have no roots or internal pipes. Instead, every cell of the gametophyte can absorb water directly from the environment, which is why they thrive in damp places and can swell quickly when wet.

items.prompt: What is the relationship between the two partners in a lichen, such as a fungus and an alga?

options.label: Symbiotic
options.feedback: Correct. A lichen is a mutualistic symbiosis: the fungus provides structure and absorbs water, while the alga makes food via photosynthesis, and both benefit.

options.label: Parasitic
options.feedback: In a parasite-host relationship, one partner is harmed; here both partners benefit, so it is not parasitic.

options.label: Competitive
options.feedback: Competition means both are struggling for the same resource; in a lichen they cooperate instead of competing.

options.label: Predatory
options.feedback: Predation is one organism eating another; the fungus and alga do not consume each other.

items.ok_line: A lichen is a symbiotic partnership, not one-sided.
items.ko_line: Both partners gain, so it is mutualism, not parasitism.
items.exp_text: In a lichen, a fungus (usually an ascomycete) forms a body that shelters an alga or a cyanobacterium. The fungus collects water and minerals, while the alga makes sugars through photosynthesis, and both share the benefits.

items.prompt: What is the flat, leaf-like part of a lichen called that helps it absorb water and light?

options.label: The rhizoid
options.feedback: Rhizoids are found in mosses, not lichens; lichens use different anchoring structures.

options.label: The capsule
options.feedback: Capsules are spore-containing structures in mosses; lichens do not have them.

options.label: The seta
options.feedback: A seta is a moss stalk; lichens have no such stalk.

options.label: The thallus
options.feedback: Correct. The thallus is the body of the lichen, which can be flat (crustose or foliose) or branched, and it performs absorption and photosynthesis.

items.ok_line: The thallus is the body of a lichen.
items.ko_line: Rhizoids, capsules, and setae belong to mosses, not lichens.
items.exp_text: The lichen's visible body is called the thallus. It is made of fungal filaments intertwined with algal cells, and its shape varies from flat crusts to leafy lobes or upright stalks, all designed to catch light and water.

items.prompt: Which partner in a lichen is responsible for making food through photosynthesis?

options.label: The fungus
options.feedback: Fungi do not have chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesize; they receive food instead.

options.label: Both equally
options.feedback: Only the photobiont (alga or cyanobacterium) can photosynthesize; the fungus cannot.

options.label: The alga
options.feedback: Correct. The algal (or cyanobacterial) partner contains chlorophyll and produces sugars, which the fungus uses as a food source.

options.label: The thallus
options.feedback: The thallus is the whole body, but only the alga inside it performs photosynthesis.

items.ok_line: The alga makes food; the fungus absorbs water.
items.ko_line: Fungi lack chlorophyll, so they rely on the alga for food.
items.exp_text: The photobiont, usually a green alga or cyanobacterium, is the green partner that uses sunlight to make carbohydrates. The fungus, which has no chlorophyll, lives off these sugars while providing a protective habitat.
